title: Purim: masks
hookLine: costumes hint at hidden faces, as God is hidden in Esther

lines: A BIBLE BOOK WITHOUT GOD'S NAME.
NO PRAYER, NO PROPHET, NO ANGEL.
cards: Start with an absence. The book of Esther, a book of the Hebrew Bible read aloud in synagogues every year, never mentions God. Not once.
In the Hebrew text there's no prayer, no prophet, no angel, no miracle a camera could film. A queen, a minister, a king who can't sleep, a lucky coincidence, and then another.
The Greek version of the book, made in ancient times, adds prayers. But in the Hebrew, the silence stays. And Purim's costumes, some teachers say, are a way of dressing up in that silence.

teach.b: In tractate Chullin, the rabbis ask a riddle: where is Esther hinted at in the Torah? They answer with a verse from Deuteronomy, where God says, in the old Jewish translation, "And I will surely hide My face in that day."
In Hebrew, I will surely hide is haster astir. Hear the sound? Haster.
Esther. The name of the book sounds like hiding. Esther herself is hidden, too.
When she's taken to the palace, she doesn't tell anyone she's Jewish; Mordecai told her not to. The Talmud, in Megillah, even says she was called Esther because she concealed who she was.
And the whole story runs on things that look like chance: a sleepless king who happens to have the royal chronicles read to him, and happens to hear about Mordecai saving his life.
Jewish tradition reads those coincidences as God working behind the curtain. Not absent. Hidden.
Wearing costumes on Purim is a much later custom, usually traced to Jews in Italy, where a rabbi allowed it as part of the day's joy.
Explanations came afterward, and one that teachers give is this: on Purim everyone looks like someone else, because in the story nothing was quite what it seemed. The queen was hiding who she was.
The coincidences were hiding a hand.
A mask asks the same question every time someone opens the door: who's really under there?

how: On Purim, many Jews, especially children, wear costumes to hear the Megillah and to the festive meal; the custom is described as part of the day's joy, and some teachers connect it to the hidden ways God works in the book of Esther.

games.q: you're Esther, newly taken into the palace. Mordecai has told you something. what is it?
o: tell the king who you are right away.
refuse to eat at the king's table.
games.why: she didn't tell anyone her people or her family, because Mordecai told her not to. her identity stayed under a mask until she needed it.

practice: Think gently of someone you saw this week who seemed fine, cheerful at work, funny in the group chat, and imagine what might be under that: tiredness, worry, a loss they haven't mentioned. You don't need to guess right.
Then turn it toward yourself, and quietly name one thing you've been hiding behind the words, I'm fine.

wordCard.voice: Purim. Lots, and a story where God's name is hidden and the costumes remind us to look underneath. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I will surely hide, from Deuteronomy 31:18, which the Talmud links to Esther's name.
